by_task.when: Federal exemptions are an allowable namespace and the facts establish the debtor's ownership of an estate asset.
by_task.procedure: Test 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) independently for every such asset because it covers any property. Include it alongside every matching category-specific exemption; its dollar limit restricts value, not EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply it when Federal is not allowable or ownership is not established, and do not list § 522(b), § 522(d), or § 522(m) as asset exemptions.

by_task.when: Oregon is an allowable namespace and the owned asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: Report Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) as an independent alternative in addition to any specific Oregon exemption. Its claim value is the asset value up to $400; value above $400 remains eligible for a $400 claim.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply it to real-property homesteads or homestead-sale proceeds, and do not replace or omit a matching category-specific exemption.

by_task.when: An allowable namespace contains a general exemption expressly covering any property or personal property.
by_task.procedure: Test that exemption independently for every factually owned asset and include it in addition to any category-specific exemption: 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) for any property, 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 for any property, Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) for personal property, and 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) for other personal property. Do not select only one competing alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not import a catch-all from a namespace not declared allowable, and do not apply the Illinois personal-property exemption when the facts expressly establish business rather than personal use.

by_task.when: An asset qualifies for a general monetary exemption in an allowable namespace.
by_task.procedure: Report that alternative separately from every specific exemption and cap its claim at the asset value. For 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5), use $1,475 plus unused § 522(d)(1), at most $15,425 per debtor and $30,850 for jointly owned property when both debtors have the full unused amount. Use $300 per spouse under 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123, $400 under Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p), and $4,000 per spouse under 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b). Consider each asset-exemption pair independently as the task requires.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not consume the allowance across different assets, exceed the asset's value, assume unused federal homestead allowance contrary to the facts, or double an exemption without two debtors holding interests in the property.

by_task.when: Arizona is allowable and an asset is a firearm, motor vehicle, residence, household item, apparel, or ornament.
by_task.procedure: Decide category before considering value. A firearm qualifies under Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(10) and one motor vehicle qualifies under § 33-1125(8) even when value exceeds the dollar limit. Use § 33-1125(1) only for wearing apparel; a pendant, bracelet, or other jewelry is not apparel, and § 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings. Use § 33-1101(A) as the homestead alternative when the residence condition is met.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat a statutory dollar cap as an eligibility cutoff, classify jewelry as clothing, or list § 33-1101(B)—a one-homestead/value limitation—as a separate asset exemption.

by_task.when: An Arizona asset satisfies a listed exemption category.
by_task.procedure: First preserve eligibility, then claim the lesser of the asset value and the applicable cap: $2,000 for firearms under § 33-1125(10), $15,000 for one motor vehicle under § 33-1125(8), and $400,000 for a qualifying homestead under § 33-1101(A). Apply the stated category limits to other provisions and report only genuinely matching categories.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not return no exemption merely because value exceeds a cap, treat a pendant or bracelet as wearing apparel, extend the ring provision beyond engagement or wedding rings, or add § 33-1101(B) as another alternative.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and an asset is evaluated under a category-specific subsection of 11 U.S.C. § 522(d).
by_task.procedure: Match the asset to the subsection's enumerated category and keep eligibility separate from value. Section 522(d)(3) covers its listed household classes, § 522(d)(4) covers jewelry, and a value above the stated cap remains eligible. A firearm is neither wearing apparel nor jewelry and is not within § 522(d)(3), though it may independently qualify under § 522(d)(5).
by_task.avoid_when: Do not infer a listed category merely from personal use, misclassify a firearm as apparel or jewelry, or omit a matching subsection solely because the asset exceeds its cap.

by_task.when: A federal category-specific exemption applies and a numeric claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: Use the lesser of asset value and the subsection's limit: $4,450 for one motor vehicle under § 522(d)(2), $700 per particular item under § 522(d)(3), $1,875 for jewelry under § 522(d)(4), and $2,800 for trade tools under § 522(d)(6). Treat the aggregate limits separately from the per-item limit and calculate § 522(d)(5) as its own alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not report full value above a per-item cap, use an aggregate ceiling as the per-item amount, or force an asset into a category solely to obtain a capped claim.

by_task.when: Illinois is allowable and the facts establish personal-use property owned by the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Test 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b)'s exemption for other personal property even when a specific exemption also applies. Also test § 12-1001(a) for necessary wearing apparel, § 12-1001(c) for a motor vehicle, and § 12-1001(e) for a professionally prescribed health aid. Include every independently applicable alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat 'other property' as unavailable merely because a specific subsection also matches. Do not use § 12-1001(d) for an ordinary household appliance or object unless the facts establish an implement, professional book, or tool of the debtor's trade.

by_task.when: An Illinois personal-property exemption applies and its claim amount is required.
by_task.procedure: Under § 12-1001(b), claim up to $4,000 per debtor, so jointly owned property may receive up to $8,000 when both spouses' exemptions apply. Under § 12-1001(c), use the lesser of the vehicle's value and $2,400 for that vehicle alternative. Sections 12-1001(a) and (e) state no dollar cap in the supplied law, so claim the asset's value while also reporting § 12-1001(b) when applicable.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the $4,000 general-property limit for the $2,400 vehicle limit, deny apparel or prescribed health aids because their specific subsection lacks a dollar cap, or apply the trade-tools subsection without supporting trade-use facts.
